The critical API misuse was bookmark sequencing: it never set a bookmark on the opener before scanning, then called seek('first-list') before that bookmark existed. verdict.failure_analysis: Trial 3 failed simple-ul, ol, existing-count-overwritten, omitted-li-closers, nested-list-counts-direct-children, incomplete-token-after-closed-list, and unsupported-after-closed-list for the same reason: it assumed seek() could be used as a safe probe for a bookmark that had not been created yet, then planned to recreate the processor and set the bookmark afterward. The relevant docs did show the right pattern under 'Recipe: scan a region before editing its opener': set a bookmark on the opener, walk forward, verify paused_at_incomplete_token() and get_last_error(), seek back, then edit. The gap is in the seek()/bookmark docs: seek() says it returns whether the cursor moved, but does not explicitly state that callers must only seek bookmarks already created successfully, nor that has_bookmark() or an explicit boolean should guard optional bookmarks. The HTML Processor set_bookmark() section also includes a Tag Processor-style optional seek example, which can imply that missing-bookmark seek is safe in this class. The trailing-incomplete and trailing-unsupported cases were not misunderstood as completion-policy cases; the candidate's bounded scan would have stopped at the end of the first list. They failed only when the missing-bookmark seek crashed before mutation.

doc_gaps.problem: The docblock says seek() returns whether the cursor moved, but does not state the precondition that the named bookmark must already exist. In current behavior, seeking a missing HTML Processor bookmark emits PHP warnings before returning false.

The docs did the important work well. The `WP_HTML_Processor` overview explicitly says text extraction is tree-aware and should use the HTML Processor, not the lexical Tag Processor. The "Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree" and `next_token()` docs explain accumulating `#text` tokens, that text may be split across tokens, and that malformed input still produces structural closers. The `next_token()` special-element exception and `get_modifiable_text()` docs explain that `SCRIPT`, `STYLE`, `TITLE`, and `TEXTAREA` do not produce child `#text` tokens, and that `TITLE`/`TEXTAREA` text is decoded while `SCRIPT`/`STYLE` is raw. The `get_modifiable_text()` docs also explicitly warn not to use that method as a predicate for ordinary text, which prevented the common mistake of including comments or script/style content.

Near-misses: trials 2 and 3 leaned on `get_token_name()` comparisons for non-text tokens without an explicit `#tag` guard. That is documented and safe here, but less crisp than the quick policy table's "match that opening tag explicitly" guidance. Trial 3 also had an unsafe byte-string fallback for Unicode truncation; the docs say to use `mb_substr(..., 'UTF-8')`, but do not spell out that `substr()` is not an acceptable fallback for code-point limits.
